```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) {
  knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
}
options(poolinfo.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
pct <- function(x) round(100 * x)
```

One trial can give several sets of site estimates, for example one for
each outcome, each subset of sites, each choice of covariates or each
effect measure. poolinfo's diagnostics describe one such set together with
its standard errors, so the same students can give different diagnostics.
In this vignette we analyze the Online Credit Recovery Study as a whole,
as Section 8 of @lee2026 does. We take its two outcomes, its two subjects,
a covariate-adjusted analysis and three first-stage analyses of passing,
and for each outcome we say what we would do next. If the informativeness
$I$, the mean reliability $\bar S$, the dispersion $H$, the logit variance
$V$ or the concentration count $J_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is new to you,
`vignette("poolinfo")` defines them, with the passing outcome as its
example.

```{r library}
library(poolinfo)
```

## The trial and its site estimates

In the summers of 2018 and 2019, the study assigned students in Los
Angeles high schools by lottery to one of two versions of their school's
summer course, an online course or the usual course directed by a teacher
[@rickles2024; @air2024]. All of them had failed Algebra 1 or English 9 in
their first year. A site is one school's course in one subject, and the
data set `ocrs` has a row for each site in which students were assigned to
both versions. We count the sites in each subject and the schools, and
summarize the sites' sizes.

```{r data}
table(ocrs$subject)
length(unique(ocrs$school))
summary(ocrs$n)
```

```{r data-facts, include = FALSE}
n_algebra <- sum(ocrs$subject == "Algebra 1")
n_schools <- length(unique(ocrs$school))
n_paired <- sum(table(ocrs$school) == 2L)
n_multi <- sum(ocrs$blocks > 1L)
stopifnot(n_algebra == 13L, n_schools == 24L, n_paired == 8L,
          all(table(ocrs$school) <= 2L), n_multi == 28L)
```

Of the `r nrow(ocrs)` sites, `r n_algebra` are in Algebra 1 and
`r nrow(ocrs) - n_algebra` in English 9. They belong to `r n_schools`
schools, so `r n_paired` schools have a site in each subject. A site has
`r min(ocrs$n)` to `r max(ocrs$n)` students, and the median site has
`r median(ocrs$n)`.

Within each site, the estimate is the coefficient of the treatment
indicator in a least squares regression of the outcome on that indicator
and the randomization blocks, with the HC2 standard error. This
coefficient is a weighted average of the blocks' differences between the
two courses, with weights proportional to $n_k p_k (1 - p_k)$, where $n_k$
is the size of block $k$ and $p_k$ the proportion of its students assigned
to the online course. A block whose students all took the same course gets
no weight. An average effect over all the site's students would weight
each block by its size $n_k$ instead, and the two weightings differ in all
`r n_multi` sites that have more than one block [@lee2026, Section 8 and
Appendix G]. Each estimate is therefore a block-adjusted contrast, which
can differ from the effect averaged over the site's students.

`ocrs` contains five sets of site estimates, each with its standard
errors:

- `estimate`, `se`: course passing, as the block-adjusted difference in
  the proportions passing.
- `estimate_adjusted`, `se_adjusted`: the same regression with four
  baseline covariates added, the grade 8 state test score in the subject
  and the grade 9 GPA, each with an indicator of a missing value.
- `estimate_credits`, `se_credits`: credits earned in the subject by the
  end of the fourth year of high school, from the same regression as
  `estimate`.
- `estimate_unadjusted`, `se_unadjusted`: the difference in the
  proportions passing between the two courses, ignoring the blocks.
- `log_odds_ratio`, `se_log_odds_ratio`: the log odds ratio of passing,
  from the same table of course by outcome as the unadjusted difference,
  so it ignores the blocks too.

`?ocrs` describes how each pair was computed from the study's public-use
file. If you start from student records of your own, you compute such
estimates and standard errors site by site and then pass them to poolinfo.

## Outcomes, subjects and covariates

We fit the posterior for passing in all `r nrow(ocrs)` sites and in each
subject, for adjusted passing and for credits. Each fit records the scale
of its effects and the estimand at each site (`scale_label` and
`target_label`), which the table at the end repeats, and
`compare_profiles()` collects the fits.

```{r fits}
rd <- "risk difference"
itt <- "the block-adjusted intention-to-treat contrast for course passing"
fit_passing <- function(data) {
  reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, site = site, data = data,
                        scale_label = rd, target_label = itt)
}
algebra <- ocrs$subject == "Algebra 1"
fits <- list(
  passing = fit_passing(ocrs),
  `passing, Algebra 1` = fit_passing(ocrs[algebra, ]),
  `passing, English 9` = fit_passing(ocrs[!algebra, ]),
  `passing, adjusted` = reliability_posterior(
    estimate_adjusted, se = se_adjusted, site = site, data = ocrs,
    scale_label = rd,
    target_label = "the covariate-adjusted contrast for course passing"
  ),
  credits = reliability_posterior(
    estimate_credits, se = se_credits, site = site, data = ocrs,
    scale_label = "credit",
    target_label = "the block-adjusted contrast for credits by year 4"
  )
)
comparison <- compare_profiles(.list = fits)
comparison
```

```{r fits-facts, include = FALSE}
tab <- as.data.frame(comparison)
rownames(tab) <- tab$analysis
stat <- function(fit, q, col = "mean") {
  ps <- profile_summary(fit)
  ps[[col]][ps$quantity == q]
}
S_pass <- site_table(fits$passing)$reliability
S_cred <- site_table(fits$credits)$reliability
p_pass <- prob_above(fits$passing)
p_cred <- prob_above(fits$credits)
gm <- function(se) exp(mean(log(se)))
grew <- sum(ocrs$se_adjusted > ocrs$se)
adjusted <- fits[["passing, adjusted"]]
width <- function(analysis) tab[analysis, "I_upper"] - tab[analysis, "I_lower"]
stopifnot(
  all(vapply(fits, function(f) all(f$checks$status == "ok"), NA)),
  p_pass > 0.95, p_cred < 0.15,
  tab["passing", "mean"] < tab["passing", "I"],
  tab["credits", "mean"] > tab["credits", "I"],
  stat(fits$passing, "effect_mean", "upper") < 0,
  stat(fits$credits, "effect_mean", "lower") < 0,
  stat(fits$credits, "effect_mean", "upper") > 0,
  tab["passing, adjusted", "I"] < tab["passing", "I"],
  grew > nrow(ocrs) / 2, gm(ocrs$se_adjusted) > gm(ocrs$se),
  stat(adjusted, "sigma_tau") < stat(fits$passing, "sigma_tau"),
  width("passing, Algebra 1") > width("passing"),
  width("passing, English 9") > width("passing")
)
```

Of these analyses, the two outcomes differ most. For passing, the
posterior mean of $I$ is `r num(tab["passing", "I"])` (95% posterior interval
`r num(tab["passing", "I_lower"])` to `r num(tab["passing", "I_upper"])`),
so a site with the geometric-mean standard error keeps about
`r pct(tab["passing", "I"])`% of its own estimate. For credits, $I$ is
`r num(tab["credits", "I"])`
(`r num(tab["credits", "I_lower"])` to `r num(tab["credits", "I_upper"])`),
and such a site keeps only about `r pct(tab["credits", "I"])`% of its
estimate. The posterior probability that $I$ exceeds 1/2, the value at
which the model would move such a site halfway toward the mean effect,
is `r num(p_pass)` for passing and `r num(p_cred)` for
credits, with 1/2 as a reference point only. Site by site, the
reliabilities run from `r num(min(S_pass))` to `r num(max(S_pass))` for
passing and from `r num(min(S_cred))` to `r num(max(S_cred))` for credits,
and the concentration counts are `r num(tab["passing", "J_eff"], 1)` and
`r num(tab["credits", "J_eff"], 1)` of `r nrow(ocrs)`. For passing the
mean reliability is a little below $I$
(`r num(tab["passing", "mean"], 3)` against
`r num(tab["passing", "I"], 3)`), and for credits a little above it
(`r num(tab["credits", "mean"], 3)` against
`r num(tab["credits", "I"], 3)`). These are the directions that the
leading term of $\bar S - I$ gives when $I$ is above or below 1/2.

In the average site, assignment to the online course lowered the
proportion passing by
`r num(-100 * stat(fits$passing, "effect_mean"), 1)` percentage points
(95% posterior interval
`r num(-100 * stat(fits$passing, "effect_mean", "upper"), 1)` to
`r num(-100 * stat(fits$passing, "effect_mean", "lower"), 1)`). Its
effect on the credits earned has a posterior mean of
`r num(stat(fits$credits, "effect_mean"), 1)` credits
(`r num(stat(fits$credits, "effect_mean", "lower"), 1)` to
`r num(stat(fits$credits, "effect_mean", "upper"), 1)`).

These diagnostics lead us to different next steps for the two outcomes.
As @lee2026 concludes, the passing profile supports a closer look at the
effects of the individual sites, starting from the posterior means and
intervals of `site_table()`. Ranking the sites would still call for its
own measure of uncertainty, because the diagnostics describe the
estimates as a whole. The credits profile gives a more uncertain basis
for such an analysis, and for credits we would report the mean effect
and the between-site standard deviation before turning to individual
sites.

Adding the baseline covariates lowers $I$ for passing from
`r num(tab["passing", "I"], 3)` to
`r num(tab["passing, adjusted", "I"], 3)`. Covariates that predict the
outcome usually shrink the standard errors, which would raise $I$. Here,
though, the HC2 standard errors grew in `r grew` of the `r nrow(ocrs)`
sites, and their geometric mean rose from `r num(gm(ocrs$se), 3)` to
`r num(gm(ocrs$se_adjusted), 3)`. Meanwhile the posterior mean of
$\sigma_\tau$ fell a little, from
`r num(stat(fits$passing, "sigma_tau"), 3)` to
`r num(stat(adjusted, "sigma_tau"), 3)`. Each analysis is conditional on
its own standard errors, so a first-stage choice that changes them
changes the diagnostics too.

Each subject's analysis describes its own set of sites and has its own
between-site standard deviation. With `r n_algebra` and
`r nrow(ocrs) - n_algebra` sites, their posterior intervals for $I$ are
wider than the pooled one: `r num(tab["passing, Algebra 1", "I_lower"])`
to `r num(tab["passing, Algebra 1", "I_upper"])` for Algebra 1 and
`r num(tab["passing, English 9", "I_lower"])` to
`r num(tab["passing, English 9", "I_upper"])` for English 9. To analyze
all `r nrow(ocrs)` sites together while letting the two subjects have
different mean effects, we put the subject in the mean model instead. Each
site is then pulled toward the mean of its subject, and $\sigma_\tau$
describes the variation around the two means.

```{r by-subject}
by_subject <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, site = site,
                                    data = ocrs, mean_model = ~ subject)
by_subject
```

```{r by-subject-facts, include = FALSE}
english <- function(col) stat(by_subject, "coef_subjectEnglish 9", col)
stopifnot(
  all(by_subject$checks$status == "ok"),
  english("mean") < 0, english("lower") < 0, english("upper") > 0,
  abs(stat(by_subject, "sigma_tau") - stat(fits$passing, "sigma_tau")) < 0.001,
  abs(stat(by_subject, "I") - tab["passing", "I"]) < 0.002
)
```

In this fit the English 9 sites' mean effect is
`r num(-100 * english("mean"), 1)` percentage points below that of the
Algebra 1 sites, with a 95% posterior interval for the difference from
`r num(-100 * english("lower"), 1)` points below to
`r num(100 * english("upper"), 1)` points above. With $\sigma_\tau$ at
`r num(stat(by_subject, "sigma_tau"), 3)`, as with a common mean, $I$ is
`r num(stat(by_subject, "I"), 3)` against `r num(tab["passing", "I"], 3)`,
so taking out the difference between the subjects leaves the variation
between sites where it was.

## Posteriors of the informativeness

Next we compare the posterior densities of $I$ for the two outcomes. We
keep the pair of fits in `outcomes`, which also gives the table at the end.

```{r densities, fig.alt = "Posterior densities of the informativeness for passing and for credits, each with its posterior mean as a solid line, its value at the posterior mean of sigma_tau squared as a dashed line and its 95% posterior interval shaded; the credits density rises steeply at 0."}
outcomes <- compare_profiles(passing = fits$passing, credits = fits$credits)
plot_functionals(outcomes)
```

```{r density-facts, include = FALSE}
# Under flat priors on the mean and on sigma_tau, the posterior density of
# sigma_tau is proportional to the restricted likelihood, computed here.
log_rl <- function(s, y, v) {
  w <- 1 / (s^2 + v)
  mu <- sum(w * y) / sum(w)
  0.5 * (sum(log(w)) - log(sum(w)) - sum(w * (y - mu)^2))
}
height_at_0 <- function(y, se) {
  peak <- optimize(log_rl, c(0, 10 * (max(abs(y)) + max(se))), y = y,
                   v = se^2, maximum = TRUE)
  exp(log_rl(0, y, se^2) - peak$objective)
}
h_pass <- height_at_0(ocrs$estimate, ocrs$se)
h_cred <- height_at_0(ocrs$estimate_credits, ocrs$se_credits)
dens <- functional_density(fits$credits, "sigma_tau", n = 2000)
gap_of <- function(fit, col) {
  g <- plugin_gap(fit)
  g[[col]][g$functional == "I"]
}
stopifnot(
  h_pass < 1e-6, h_cred > 0.05, h_cred < 0.15,
  abs(dens$density[1] / max(dens$density) - h_cred) < 0.01,
  tab["passing", "I_lower"] < tab["credits", "I_upper"],
  gap_of(fits$passing, "difference") > 0,
  gap_of(fits$credits, "difference") > gap_of(fits$passing, "difference")
)
```

The shaded 95% posterior intervals overlap only between
`r num(tab["passing", "I_lower"])` and `r num(tab["credits", "I_upper"])`.
At the left edge the credits density rises without bound, and the plot
cuts it off. This happens in every analysis under the flat prior, because
the posterior density of $\sigma_\tau$ is positive at 0 and, near 0, $I$
grows like $\sigma_\tau^2$. How much of it shows depends on how high the
posterior of $\sigma_\tau$ is at 0. For passing that height is about
`r sprintf("$10^{%d}$", round(log10(h_pass)))` of the posterior's peak, so
nothing is visible, but for credits it is `r num(h_cred)` of the peak.

Dashed lines mark $I$ at the posterior mean of $\sigma_\tau^2$,
`r num(gap_of(fits$passing, "at_mean_sigma2"), 3)` for passing and
`r num(gap_of(fits$credits, "at_mean_sigma2"), 3)` for credits. Both lie
right of the solid lines, the posterior means, because $I$ is a concave
function of $\sigma_\tau^2$ [@lee2026, Proposition 3], and the gap is
`r num(gap_of(fits$passing, "difference"), 3)` for passing and
`r num(gap_of(fits$credits, "difference"), 3)` for credits.

## The contrast and the effect measure

Reporting the effects in percentage points rather than proportions
multiplies every estimate and standard error by 100. Under the flat prior
the diagnostics stay the same, because $\sigma_\tau$ grows by the same
factor as the standard errors [@lee2026, Appendix G]; a proper prior
would need its scale multiplied too. A different contrast or a different
effect measure is another kind of change, since it alters the spread of
the true effects and the standard errors in different ways. We compare
three analyses of passing: the block-adjusted difference used so far, the
unadjusted difference in the proportions passing, and the log odds ratio.
Both of the last two come from the same table of course by outcome in
each site, so the step between them changes the effect measure alone.

```{r scales}
unadjusted <- reliability_posterior(estimate_unadjusted, se = se_unadjusted,
                                    data = ocrs)
log_odds <- reliability_posterior(log_odds_ratio, se = se_log_odds_ratio,
                                  data = ocrs)
scales <- compare_profiles(`difference, block-adjusted` = fits$passing,
                           `difference, unadjusted` = unadjusted,
                           `log odds ratio` = log_odds)
scales
```

```{r scale-facts, include = FALSE}
st <- as.data.frame(scales)
rownames(st) <- c("block", "unadjusted", "lor")
in_points <- reliability_posterior(100 * estimate, se = 100 * se, data = ocrs)
# The contour band of the leading term of H at each point of the plane,
# and the band of each posterior mean of H: 2 is between 0.02 and 0.03.
band <- floor(100 * 0.5 * st$I * (1 - st$I) * st$V)
stopifnot(
  abs(stat(in_points, "I") - st["block", "I"]) < 1e-8,
  st["block", "I"] > st["unadjusted", "I"],
  st["unadjusted", "I"] > st["lor", "I"], st["lor", "I"] > 0.5,
  st["lor", "V"] > st["block", "V"], st["block", "V"] > st["unadjusted", "V"],
  identical(band, c(2, 2, 3)), identical(floor(100 * st$H), band)
)
```

Dropping the blocks lowers $I$ from `r num(st["block", "I"], 3)` to
`r num(st["unadjusted", "I"], 3)`, and the log odds ratio lowers it again,
to `r num(st["lor", "I"], 3)`, with a posterior probability of
`r num(prob_above(log_odds))` that $I$ exceeds 1/2. Next we place the
three analyses in the plane of $I$ and $V$, with contours of the leading
term of the dispersion, $I(1 - I)V/2$.

```{r plane, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "The three analyses of passing as points in the plane of the informativeness and the logit variance, each with the 95% posterior interval of its informativeness; the log odds ratio lies higher and further left than the two differences."}
plot(scales, type = "plane")
```

The log odds ratio lies above the two differences in the plane, at
$V = `r num(st["lor", "V"])`$ against `r num(st["unadjusted", "V"])` for
the unadjusted difference and `r num(st["block", "V"])` for the
block-adjusted one. Its sampling variance grows as a site's passing
proportions approach 0 or 1, whereas a difference's is largest when they
are near 1/2, so the two measures spread the same sites' standard errors
differently. Both differences lie between the contours at
`r num(band[1] / 100)` and `r num(band[1] / 100 + 0.01)`, and the log odds
ratio between `r num(band[3] / 100)` and `r num(band[3] / 100 + 0.01)`, in
line with their dispersions of `r num(st["block", "H"], 3)`,
`r num(st["unadjusted", "H"], 3)` and `r num(st["lor", "H"], 3)`. In a
report we would name both the contrast and the effect measure, as the
labels of the fits for the outcomes do.

## Schools with two sites

Each of the `r n_paired` schools with a site in each subject contributes
two estimates, and some of its students appear in both, while the model
treats all `r nrow(ocrs)` sites as independent. Each site also counts once
in the diagnostics, whatever its size, so these schools count twice. To
see how much this matters, we keep one site of each such school, in all
$2^{`r n_paired`} = `r 2^n_paired`$ ways, and refit both outcomes to each
set of `r nrow(ocrs) - n_paired` sites.

```{r schools}
paired <- as.integer(names(which(table(ocrs$school) == 2)))
choices <- expand.grid(rep(list(c("Algebra 1", "English 9")), length(paired)))
I_of <- function(fit) subset(profile_summary(fit), quantity == "I")$mean
I_subsets <- t(apply(choices, 1, function(subject) {
  keep <- !(ocrs$school %in% paired) |
    paste(ocrs$school, ocrs$subject) %in% paste(paired, subject)
  sites <- ocrs[keep, ]
  c(passing = I_of(reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, data = sites)),
    credits = I_of(reliability_posterior(estimate_credits, se = se_credits,
                                         data = sites)))
}))
apply(I_subsets, 2, range)
```

```{r schools-facts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(nrow(I_subsets) == 2^n_paired,
          all(I_subsets[, "passing"] > 0.5), all(I_subsets[, "credits"] < 0.5))
```

Across the `r nrow(I_subsets)` sets of `r nrow(ocrs) - n_paired` sites,
the posterior mean of $I$ runs from `r num(min(I_subsets[, "passing"]), 3)`
to `r num(max(I_subsets[, "passing"]), 3)` for passing and from
`r num(min(I_subsets[, "credits"]), 3)` to
`r num(max(I_subsets[, "credits"]), 3)` for credits, against
`r num(tab["passing", "I"], 3)` and `r num(tab["credits", "I"], 3)` with
all `r nrow(ocrs)` sites. Passing stays above 1/2 and credits below it in
every set, so the contrast between the outcomes survives whichever site of
a paired school we keep. These refits vary the set of sites. Allowing for
the students who appear in both of a school's sites would take a model
with the covariance between the school's two estimates, which the working
model leaves out [@lee2026, Section 9].

## A table for the report

`report_table()` lays out a comparison in the format of Table 5 of
@lee2026 and adds a note for the readers of the report. We make the table
for the two outcomes.

```{r table, results = "asis"}
cat(report_table(outcomes, format = "markdown"))
```

The note under the table carries the scale and the estimand that we set
for each outcome. Called with `comparison`, `report_table()` makes the
table for all five analyses, and with `format = "latex"` it writes the
table as LaTeX code with the rules of the booktabs package.
